content: Images uploaded to WikiDoc must be properly tagged to comply with copyright laws and to identify materials that are free for use. Since WikiDoc servers are based in the United States, only U.S. copyright law is applicable when national laws are relevant. Below are detailed guidelines for tagging images: 1. Tagging Images: Each image must be tagged on its description page using one of the provided tags. This helps track the copyright status of the image. Tags should be placed on a separate line within the description page. For guidance on where to place these tags, refer to the Template messages section. If an image is categorized under a vague tag (e.g., CopyrightedFreeUse), you should specify the exact license or permission details. For images requiring attribution, clearly state who must be credited. Note that the GNU Free Documentation License (GFDL) mandates attribution. If an image falls under multiple categories, include all applicable tags. Always provide detailed information about the source or copyright holder of the image. While Wikimedia Commons does not permit fair use images, such images can still be used on WikiDoc. However, fair use laws vary by country, and some images may need to be excluded from certain distributions, such as Mandriva Linux. 2. For Image Creators: If you are the original creator of an image (e.g., photographer or designer), you are encouraged to license your work under a free license with minimal restrictions. Free licenses, often referred to as copyleft, aim to keep your work freely accessible while protecting its use. Examples of free licenses include: {{GFDL-self}}: The GNU Free Documentation License, created by the Free Software Foundation, originally intended for free software documentation. {{cc-by-sa-2.5}}: The Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike license, which allows free use (including commercial use) as long as the creator is credited and derivative works are shared under the same license. {{pd-self}}: Public Domain, though there is some legal ambiguity about whether creators can release their work into the public domain. {{No rights reserved}}: A license developed to address the legal uncertainties of public domain releases. Creators may apply multiple licenses to their work, but care should be taken to avoid contradictory licenses. If you have questions or need assistance, members of the WikiDoc project are available to help. 3. Public Domain Images: Most images found online are not in the public domain, even if no explicit copyright information is provided. Images qualify as public domain only if they meet specific criteria, such as being very old, created by certain government employees, or explicitly released into the public domain by the author. For a detailed chart on U.S. public domain regulations, refer to the provided resources. 4. Presumed Free Images: {{GFDL-presumed}}: This tag is used for images believed to be free of copyright issues, often because they were uploaded by the creator. This is particularly relevant for images uploaded before mid-2004, when copyright tagging was not mandatory. 5. Tags for Deprecated Images: Unfree Images: {{PUIdisputed}}: Used for images with disputed copyright status. If unresolved, the image is typically deleted after 14 days. {{PUInonfree}}: Used for images with a non-free license. If no alternative license is found, the image is deleted after 14 days. In both cases, the uploader's talk page should be updated with the appropriate notification, and the image should be listed on the Possibly unfree images page for further review. Copyright Violations: Images that violate copyright laws are marked for quick deletion. The uploader's talk page should be updated with a notification template. Bad Images: {{Missing image}}: Used for images that cannot be deleted through standard procedures due to software issues. These images require manual deletion by a developer. 6. Creating New Tags or Sub-Categories: If you are uploading a large collection of images, consider creating a new tag and sub-category. Before creating a new tag, propose it on the Image copyright tags discussion page to avoid issues such as redundancy or vagueness. Add the category Image copyright tags to the template by including the appropriate code at the bottom. 7. Image Template Notice: Each copyright tag (e.g., {{Fairuse}}) should correspond to a specific category. Placing a tag on an image will automatically categorize it, as the template is linked to the category. For example, the {{Fairuse}} tag should include a notice using the {{Image template notice|Fairuse}} template.
